Exploratory Common-Factor Analysis With Confidence Intervals

Source: R/fa_exploratory.R
fa_exploratory.Rd

Fits a common-factor model, with rotation and uncertainty for its rotated loadings. This is an exploratory measurement model: every item can load on every factor. The estimates and rotation-aware standard errors are computed by lavaan, which is required; DMAR adds the table and its intervals, the display, the refusals, and the fit measure policy. The function does not compute principal components. It carries a name of its own so that attaching lavaan, whose efa() it calls, masks nothing. efa_k() is the same function under a shorter name, as cfa_k() is for fa_confirmatory.

Usage

fa_exploratory(
  data = NULL,
  nfactors = 1L,
  S = NULL,
  N = NULL,
  items = NULL,
  estimator = "ML",
  missing = "fiml",
  ordered = NULL,
  rotation = "oblimin",
  target = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  rmsea_conf_level = 0.9,
  seed = NULL,
  point_estimates_only = FALSE
)

efa_k(
  data = NULL,
  nfactors = 1L,
  S = NULL,
  N = NULL,
  items = NULL,
  estimator = "ML",
  missing = "fiml",
  ordered = NULL,
  rotation = "oblimin",
  target = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  rmsea_conf_level = 0.9,
  seed = NULL,
  point_estimates_only = FALSE
)

# S3 method for class 'dmar_fa_exploratory'
print(x, digits = getOption("dmar.digits", 3L), ...)

Arguments

data

Numeric raw observations. Supply exactly one of data or S.

nfactors

Number of common factors, a positive integer giving an identified exploratory model. With a target, its number of factors when nfactors is not supplied; a supplied value must agree with it.

S

Named positive definite covariance matrix, with N. A correlation matrix is a covariance matrix with unit variances, and the original metric then coincides with the standardized one.

N

Sample size for covariance input.

items

The items to analyze, by name: columns of data, or rows and columns of S, which is then reduced to them, in the order given; only the reduced matrix need be finite and positive definite. NULL, the default, analyzes every column of data or of S, or, with a target, the items the target names. Names that cannot be read as at least three distinct items are refused with an error of class dmar_items_invalid (see dmar_metadata).

estimator

"ML" (default) or "MLR" for continuous items; "ULS" for the minimum residual (minres) solution of Harman and Jones (1966), unweighted least squares fitted to the correlation matrix (see Details); explicitly request "WLSMV" for ordered items. MLR uses the same likelihood estimates with Huber-White sandwich errors.

missing

"fiml" (default), "ml", or "listwise" for continuous items under ML or MLR. With ordered items the default fits the items as they stand when no item value is missing, as fa_confirmatory does; with missing values ordered items require an explicit "pairwise" or "listwise" choice, and FIML is not substituted with deletion. ULS has no likelihood, so it takes complete raw data, an explicit "listwise" choice, or a correlation matrix estimated elsewhere through S (for example the maximum likelihood estimate of cov_fiml); with incomplete data the default "fiml" is refused rather than replaced. Covariance input has no missing-data route.

ordered

NULL, TRUE for all items, or their names.

rotation

The rotation criterion, by name. Oblique, the factors free to correlate: "oblimin" (default; direct oblimin with gamma 0, Jennrich & Sampson, 1966), "quartimin" (Carroll, 1953), "geomin" (Yates, 1987; epsilon 0.001), "simplimax" (Kiers, 1994), "oblimax" (Saunders, 1961), "infomax" (McKeon, 1968, as Browne, 2001, presents it), and "bentler" (Bentler, 1977). Orthogonal, the factors kept uncorrelated: "varimax" (Kaiser, 1958; with Kaiser row weights, as lavaan applies it) and "quartimax" (Neuhaus & Wrigley, 1954). "target" and "target_orthogonal" rotate to the partially specified target given in target, the factors free to correlate (Browne, 1972b) or kept uncorrelated (Browne, 1972a); see Details. "none" returns the unrotated solution lavaan identifies, whose factors are uncorrelated. Each criterion is applied in the form named here by lavaan's gradient projection algorithm from 30 random starts; Browne (2001) reviews the family.

target

For rotation = "target" or "target_orthogonal", the partially specified target, in either of two forms (NULL, the default, for every other rotation). The usual one is a named list of item keys, the form fa_confirmatory takes for factors: each element names a factor and the items expected to load on it. An item keyed to a factor is targeted at 0 on every factor it is not keyed to and left unspecified on the factors it is keyed to (an item keyed to two factors is unspecified on both), and an analyzed item keyed to no factor is unspecified on every factor. The other is a numeric matrix of items by factors, with the items as row names in any order, NA for each unspecified loading, and elsewhere a target value for the standardized pattern loading, strictly between -1 and 1 (see Details); column names, if given, name the factors.

conf_level

Confidence level of the intervals for the parameters, the communalities, and the determinacy and H, default 0.95.

rmsea_conf_level

Confidence level of the RMSEA interval on the fit line and in the fit_measures attribute (with the gamma hat and adjusted gamma hat intervals there, which come from the same noncentrality limits), default 0.90, the conventional level, whose limits decide the tests of close and not close fit at .05 (see sem_fit_measures); rmsea_conf_level = 0.95 gives a 95 percent interval. It is separate from conf_level, which does not reach the RMSEA.

seed

Optional seed for rotation starts; default NULL uses the current random stream. A supplied seed restores the caller's stream.

point_estimates_only

FALSE (default) for the full analysis; TRUE for the same estimates without their standard errors, tests, and intervals, which are then not computed (see Details), for a program that needs only the estimates and wants them sooner.

x

For print(), a table returned by fa_exploratory().

digits

For print(), the decimal places of the display (default getOption("dmar.digits", 3); see dmar_tbl).

...

For print(), passed to print.data.frame().

Value

A dmar_tbl data frame (classes dmar_fa_exploratory and dmar_factor_analysis) with term, the parameter labels lhs, op, and rhs, estimate, se, statistic, p_value, ci_lower, ci_upper, conf_level, and metric: the parameters in the original metric, the standardized solution, the communalities (op "communality"), Hofmann's complexity (op "complexity", with no interval), and each factor's determinacy and coefficient H (ops "determinacy" and "H", the factor as both lhs and rhs). Attributes retain fit (the lavaan object), method (sample size, estimator, standard error and missing data methods, the rotation and whether it is orthogonal, the fitted structure, and for a target rotation the target and the number of loadings it specifies), variance_accounted, factor_quality, eligible fit_measures (a sem_fit_measures table, whose RMSEA interval is at rmsea_conf_level), rmsea_conf_level, and point_estimates_only (TRUE or FALSE, as called). tidy() preserves the parameter rows; glance() reports the analysis method and sample size, and both carry point_estimates_only as a column; print() shows the display described in Details.

Details

The model is fitted to the covariance matrix of the items, with their means under FIML, and the standardized solution is derived from it (Cudeck, 1989, on why a correlation matrix is not analyzed as if it were a covariance matrix); the table carries both metrics. Two routes are correlation structures by construction: the minimum residual solution, which is defined on the correlation matrix and is not invariant to the scale of the items, and the WLSMV analysis of ordered items, which fits their polychoric correlations and thresholds.

FIML fits the raw incomplete observations directly, under a normal working likelihood and missingness at random given the included items. It does not treat an estimated unrestricted covariance matrix as if it were an ordinary complete-data sample covariance. Factor signs and order are arbitrary. Wald intervals describe the selected rotated solution, conditional on the requested factor count; they do not include uncertainty from choosing that count or rotation.

Display. The printed result, and knit_print() and as_kable of it, show the solution rather than the parameter list: one row per item with its standardized pattern loading on each factor and that loading's interval, its communality with its interval, and its complexity; above the table the sample, estimator, missing data method, rotation and its form, and standard error method; beneath it the variance each factor accounts for, the factor correlations with their intervals (or the statement that the rotation fixed them at zero), each factor's determinacy and coefficient H with their intervals, and the fit. The table itself keeps every parameter in both metrics, which tidy() returns, and a subset of it prints as an ordinary DMAR table.

Hofmann's (1978) complexity of an item is the square of the sum of its squared pattern loadings divided by the sum of its loadings to the fourth power: 1 for an item that loads on one factor alone, and the number of factors for an item that loads equally on all of them. The variance a factor accounts for is its diagonal element of Phi Lambda' Lambda, with Lambda the standardized pattern loadings and Phi the factor correlation matrix (the column sum of squared loadings when the factors are uncorrelated); these sum to the sum of the communalities, and each is also given as a proportion of the total variance of the items (their number, in the standardized metric) and of the common variance. No cumulative column is shown, since the order of the factors is arbitrary. The variance_accounted attribute holds this table. The fit line reads the fit_measures attribute: the chi square statistic with its degrees of freedom and p-value, the RMSEA with its interval at rmsea_conf_level (90 percent by default), which the line names, the CFI, TLI, and SRMR, and the version lines that say which indices they are (see sem_fit_measures); under ULS it gives the discrepancy statistic, the NFI, and the SRMR (below). The measures are computed from the unrotated solution of the same model: the chi square statistic and the standard indices do not depend on the rotation, but lavaan's FIML-corrected indices of a rotated object do, since its rotated parameterization counts more free parameters than the model has, so the fit of a rotated solution is taken from the unrotated fit, and every rotation reports the same fit.

Rotation to a partially specified target. A partially specified target states what is expected of some loadings and nothing of the rest: each loading is either given a target value or left unspecified. The rotation minimizes the sum of squared differences between the specified loadings and their target values, in the standardized metric, and asks nothing of the unspecified ones (Browne, 2001, p. 124). Zeros are the usual specification, since which loadings should be near zero is easier to say than how large the others should be (Browne, 2001, p. 124); the list form of target specifies exactly those, a zero for each item on each factor it is not keyed to. Unlike a confirmatory model, which forces the specified loadings to their values, the rotation brings them only as close to their targets as the data allow, so a specified zero whose rotated loading is far from zero signals a misspecified zero (Browne, 2001, pp. 124–125), and its interval in the table shows by how much. A specified value must lie strictly between -1 and 1, and a target with a value outside that range is refused: the target is stated in the standardized metric, and such a value is more likely a loading taken from an item's original metric than an expected standardized loading. No row weights are applied (Browne, 2001, p. 125, finds the Kaiser and Cureton-Mulaik row weights unsuited to a partially specified target), and the rotation is iterated to a gradient tolerance of 1e-8 rather than lavaan's 1e-5, so that zeros the rotation attains exactly (below) are attained to about that precision. The factors keep lavaan's names (f1, f2, ...) in the order of the target's columns, and the display prints the target beneath the table with the names it gave. Rotation does not change the model, so the fit is that of every other rotation.

When every specified value is zero, the sign of each factor is arbitrary, and each factor is reflected, as lavaan does by default, so that its loadings have a positive sum. Since lavaan reflects all the factors or none, no factor is reflected when any specified value is nonzero. A factor whose column holds a nonzero value then takes its sign from the target (a negative target keeps its sign), but a factor whose specified values are all zero takes the sign of the random start from which the rotation reached its minimum. A supplied seed fixes that sign; with seed = NULL the loadings of such a factor, and its correlations with the other factors, can change sign from one run to the next. Either sign gives the same solution, so such a factor may be read with its loadings and its correlations reversed together.

The target must identify the rotation, and lavaan does not check that it does: an unidentified rotation comes back with finite standard errors and no warning. DMAR checks the conditions of Algina (1980) before reporting. In oblique rotation each factor's column needs at least m - 1 specified zeros, for m factors, and the standardized unrotated loadings of the items specified in it must have rank m - 1 (Browne, 2001, p. 115; Algina, 1980, Theorem 2). A column with a nonzero target value needs one entry more, m entries with rank m (Theorem 1): with the factor variances at one, m - 1 restrictions that include a nonzero value need not identify the rotation, as Algina (1980, pp. 393–394) shows by example, so DMAR asks for the larger count. In orthogonal rotation fewer suffice: taken in increasing order of their specified entries, the columns need at least 0, 1, ..., m - 1 zeros, and again a column with a nonzero value one entry more (Theorem 3), and the rank of a column's rows is checked against the same numbers. Two columns with the same specified entries and values would leave their factors indistinguishable. A target that fails is refused with an error of class dmar_target_unidentified, and one that cannot be read as a target with class dmar_target_invalid; both inherit dmar_refusal and carry a reason element (see dmar_metadata). Only a set of rows that is rank deficient to within the precision of the fitted loadings is refused (a singular value below 1e-6 times the largest); one that is nearly deficient shows itself in wide intervals.

When a column carries only the minimum number of zeros, the rotation can attain them exactly. Those loadings are then fixed by the target rather than estimated (lavaan reports a standard error of zero and a statistic that means nothing). The table shows each at its target value itself, in place of the rotated estimate, which differs from it only by the rotation's convergence error, with se, statistic, and p_value NA and both limits at the target, in both metrics. When every specified loading is attained this way, as in an oblique rotation with m - 1 zeros in every column, the rotated solution is the confirmatory factor model with those loadings fixed at their targets and the factor variances at one (the factors uncorrelated in an orthogonal rotation).

Myers, Jin, Ahn, Celimli, and Zopluoglu (2015) studied target rotation by simulation. Three factors were measured by 10 or 20 items (p. 497). The communalities were low (.20 to .40), high (.60 to .80), or wide (.20 to .80), and minor factors added error to the model (both p. 498). The target values were in error by up to two standard errors (p. 500). The errors in the target values had a negligible effect on the accuracy and the stability of the rotated loadings (pp. 502–503). Specifying more targets per factor improved both somewhat, the accuracy most when the communalities were low and the stability most when they were high (p. 502).

In their comparison with geomin, every target value was in error by two standard errors (pp. 500–501). Target rotation recovered the population loadings more accurately in all 27 comparisons, one for each number of targets at each level of communality, though by small amounts (p. 502). Their measure of accuracy was the absolute value of the bias of a replication, the signed error averaged over all the loadings (p. 501); its mean was at or below 0.10 for both rotations, and the largest difference between them was 0.08 (p. 502). Geomin gave the more stable solution in 20 of the 27, among them every comparison with low communalities; target rotation was the more stable with high communalities and six or more targets per factor, and with wide communalities and nine or more (pp. 499, 502–503). Their advice on the number of targets is to specify the target as fully as the theory allows, particularly when the items are not uniformly highly reliable indicators of the factors (p. 503). Comparing the rotations, they conclude that the extra work of specifying a target may be worthwhile for accuracy; for stability, they expect geomin to do better when the items are less than uniformly reliable indicators, and target rotation to do better when the items are uniformly reliable and several targets are specified (p. 504). Less stability is more sampling variability, which the intervals of a given analysis show.

The intervals condition on a target fixed before the data were seen. Browne (2001, pp. 125, 148) describes revising a target in sequence, leaving unspecified the entries that proved misspecified and specifying as zeros the loadings that proved near zero; such a sequence is exploratory, capitalizes on chance, and calls for a confirmatory analysis of new data. The method attribute holds the target (target, items by factors, NA where unspecified, with the target's factor names) and the number of loadings it specifies (n_specified).

Determinacy and H. The determinacy of a factor is the correlation of its regression factor score with the factor, the multiple correlation of the factor with the items (Grice, 2001; the factor determinacy index of Ferrando & Lorenzo-Seva, 2018): \(\sqrt{[\Phi \Lambda' R^{-1} \Lambda \Phi]_{kk}}\), with \(\Lambda\) the standardized pattern loadings, \(\Phi\) the factor correlations, and \(R\) the item correlation matrix the model implies. Its square is the largest reliability any weighted sum of the items reaches as a measure of the factor, which Ferrando and Lorenzo-Seva call the generalized H and bifactor_indices the maximal reliability. Coefficient H is Hancock and Mueller's (2001) closed form on the factor's standardized loadings \(l_j\) alone, \(H = (1 + (\sum_j l_j^2 / (1 - l_j^2))^{-1})^{-1}\), applied to one factor of a multidimensional solution as Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016) apply it, so that each item's variance from the other factors counts as error. With one factor H is the squared determinacy; otherwise the two can differ in either direction, and the squared determinacy is the quantity to read beside H. Both are reported for every factor with a delta method standard error over lavaan's covariance matrix of the standardized estimates (the matrix behind the standardized loading and communality intervals) and Wald limits formed on the logit scale and transformed back (Browne, 1982; the confidence interval transformation principle of Kelley, 2007: the limits of a monotone transformation of a parameter are the transformation of its limits), as reliability_H forms them by default, so they lie within (0, 1); the se column is the standard error of the index itself, and with one factor it is the standard error fa_confirmatory gives its H row for the same model fitted the same way (by FIML). For ordered items both describe the latent responses behind the categories, not composites of the observed scores (the G-H-latent of Ferrando and Lorenzo-Seva), and the display says so. Beside each determinacy \(\rho\) the display and the factor_quality attribute give \(2\rho^2 - 1\) (min_score_correlation, with its delta method standard error and the determinacy's limits mapped through it), the lowest correlation two sets of factor scores equally consistent with the model can have (Guttman, 1955, as Grice, 2001, p. 435, presents it): zero when \(\rho^2 = .5\), negative below. No line is drawn. factor_scores gives the determinacy of the Bartlett score as well, and for each missing data pattern. The factor_quality attribute holds this table.

estimator = "ULS" is the minimum residual method: the loadings and unique variances minimize the sum of squared residuals of the correlation matrix, the unique variances absorbing the diagonal, so that the off-diagonal correlations are reproduced as closely as the common factors allow (Harman & Jones, 1966; psych::fa(fm = "minres") gives the same loadings and communalities, up to the order and signs of the factors). The estimates need no distributional assumption, and the correlation matrix is the structure fitted (lavaan's correlation = TRUE), so rescaling an item does not change them. With raw data the standard errors are lavaan's sandwich for a least squares estimator with the normal theory covariance matrix of the correlations (its se = "robust.sem.nt"; Browne, 1984), and the rotation enters them as for ML. A supplied correlation or covariance matrix carries no such covariance matrix, so with S the ULS estimates and communalities are returned with their standard errors and limits NA, and the note under the table says so. The ULS statistic is in the units of the squared correlations and has no chi square reference distribution, so in the fit_measures attribute the chi_square row holds N - 1 times the ULS discrepancy with no p-value, the RMSEA rows and the CFI, TLI, RNI, and IFI are NA, and the NFI and the SRMR, which do not rest on that distribution, are reported (see sem_fit_measures); a maximum likelihood fit of the same items gives the fit indices and their inference.

The table contains original-unit parameters, standardized loadings and factor correlations, and communalities with intervals. A communality is one minus the standardized residual variance, so its interval reverses the limits of that variance. Wald limits are not clipped to [0, 1]. Improper or unidentified solutions are refused, with an error of class dmar_efa_no_solution whose reason element says whether the model did not converge, converged to an improper solution (lavaan's post-estimation check failed: a residual variance below zero, or a covariance matrix that is not positive definite), or left the rotation-aware standard errors unavailable; factor_count reads it to report such a count as a row. When a residual variance is below zero and the likelihood has no maximum at all (the likelihood flat or still rising as the variance falls, as when too many factors are extracted), the refusal says so instead (reason "no maximum", and the class dmar_no_maximum as well; see fa_bifactor for the check) and prints the lavaan::efa() code of the unrotated fit, which selects items from the data or covariance matrix given, where bounds = "pos.var", lavaan's own default, or fewer factors are the choices. When the unrestricted FIML likelihood diagnostic fails but the constrained model and its H0-based errors remain eligible, parameter results are qualified and H1-dependent fit indices are withheld. Absence of a diagnosed obstacle does not certify a unique global maximum.

Point estimates only. With point_estimates_only = TRUE the table has the rows and the estimates of the full analysis (the loadings, factor correlations, and residual variances in both metrics, the communalities, Hofmann's complexity, and each factor's determinacy and H), and so do the variance_accounted, factor_quality, and fit_measures attributes, but no standard error, test of a parameter, or interval is computed: the se, statistic, p_value, ci_lower, and ci_upper columns are NA, as are the standard errors and limits of factor_quality. lavaan is asked for no standard errors (its se = "none"), so neither the information matrix behind them (with its sandwich under MLR, WLSMV, and ULS) nor the rotation-aware errors of the rotated loadings are formed, nor the delta method errors of the standardized solution, the communalities, the determinacy, and H; and the rotated fit is made without a test statistic, which DMAR never reads, since the fit measures come from the unrotated fit. That fit keeps its test, so every fit measure is the one the full analysis reports, the robust statistic and the FIML-corrected indices under MLR and the scaled and shifted statistic under WLSMV included. conf_level then sets nothing, since the only interval left is the RMSEA interval of the fit line, at rmsea_conf_level, and the display states no other level. A loading of a target rotation that is attained exactly is recognized by lying within 1e-6 of its target, in place of its standard error of zero, and shown at the target as in the full analysis; in rare cases (a chance of the order of 1e-5 for each specified loading) an estimated loading falls that close to its target by chance and is shown at it, which the full analysis would estimate, within 1e-6 of the same value. The input and target checks, and the refusals of a solution that did not converge or is improper and of a likelihood without a maximum (whose code reproduces the full fit), are made as before. The refusal of a solution whose rotation-aware standard errors are unavailable is the full analysis's guard against a solution that is not identified at its estimates, whose estimates are then not unique; it is kept by inverting the expected information of the unrotated fit, which is cheap, and, only when that fails, the information its standard errors would use (the observed information under FIML); a solution whose information cannot be inverted is refused with the same class and reason. A failure confined to the rotation's part of the rotation-aware errors is not detected, so in that rare case the estimates are returned for a solution the full analysis refuses. A FIML fit whose standard errors would need the unavailable unrestricted (H1) information is not refused, since none are computed; its fit measures are withheld as in the full analysis, with a warning of the same class whose note speaks of the estimates alone. The display says that standard errors and intervals were not computed, the result carries the setting as its point_estimates_only attribute, and the lavaan object in fit has no standard errors (and, when rotated, no test). The time saved depends on the estimator and the data. In one set of timings with three factors under oblimin, the nine classic Holzinger and Swineford tests took about a third less time under ML and MLR (0.79 s against 0.51 s under ML) and half or more less under ULS and WLSMV (0.70 s against 0.27 s for the tests cut into five ordered categories), and the rotated solution of 18 items with 1,000 cases and 410 patterns of missing values took 29 s against 17 s under MLR with FIML, and 18 s against 9 s under ML. What remains is the estimation itself and the fit measures, chiefly the robust statistic and the FIML-corrected indices of the unrotated fit, which are kept; an unrotated analysis therefore saves little or nothing (16.5 s against 16.7 s on those 18 items), and a program that also fits the unrotated model (for its own fit measures, say) saves on the rotated fit alone: the two together took 45 s against 34 s.

Rosseel, Y. (2012). lavaan: An R package for structural equation modeling. Journal of Statistical Software, 48(2), 1–36. doi:10.18637/jss.v048.i02

Saunders, D. R. (1961). The rationale for an "oblimax" method of transformation in factor analysis. Psychometrika, 26(3), 317–324. doi:10.1007/BF02289800

Yates, A. (1987). Multivariate exploratory data analysis: A perspective on exploratory factor analysis. State University of New York Press.

See also

parallel_analysis for the factor count, fa_confirmatory for the confirmatory model, factor_scores, which takes the lavaan object in the fit attribute, and reliability_H for coefficient H of one scale with bootstrap intervals.

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

items <- c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes", "t4_lozenges",
           "t6_paragraph_comprehension", "t7_sentence", "t9_word_meaning")
two <- fa_exploratory(holzinger_swineford, nfactors = 2, items = items,
                      seed = 113)
two                       # the solution: loadings with intervals,
#> Exploratory factor analysis: 2 factors, 6 items, N = 301
#> Estimator: ML; missing data: FIML; rotation: oblimin (oblique); SE: standard
#> 
#>                        item                      f1                      f2

#>                    t2_cubes    0.443 [0.304, 0.582]   0.052 [-0.081, 0.185]
#>                 t4_lozenges    0.766 [0.629, 0.903] -0.072 [-0.125, -0.019]
#>  t6_paragraph_comprehension   0.040 [-0.032, 0.112]    0.833 [0.779, 0.888]
#>                 t7_sentence -0.088 [-0.139, -0.038]    0.899 [0.850, 0.949]
#>             t9_word_meaning    0.085 [0.009, 0.161]    0.805 [0.747, 0.863]
#>           communality complexity
#>  0.426 [0.286, 0.566]      1.341

#>  0.559 [0.333, 0.784]      1.018
#>  0.716 [0.641, 0.791]      1.005
#>  0.768 [0.690, 0.846]      1.019
#>  0.696 [0.621, 0.771]      1.022
#> (standardized pattern loadings and communalities with 95% intervals, and Hofmann's complexity; tidy(x) has every parameter in both metrics)

# An orthogonal rotation, its estimates alone: the standard errors,
# tests, and intervals are not computed, which saves time.
fa_exploratory(holzinger_swineford, nfactors = 2, items = items,
               rotation = "varimax", seed = 113, point_estimates_only = TRUE)
#> Exploratory factor analysis: 2 factors, 6 items, N = 301
#> Estimator: ML; missing data: FIML; rotation: varimax (orthogonal), Kaiser row weights; SE: not computed (point_estimates_only = TRUE)
#> 
#>                        item    f1    f2 communality complexity
#>        t1_visual_perception 0.584 0.291       0.426      1.467
#>                    t2_cubes 0.450 0.105       0.213      1.108

#> 
#> Fit: chi square 2.109, df 4, p = 0.7157; RMSEA with 90% interval 0.000 [0.000, 0.064]; CFI 1.000; TLI 1.011; SRMR 0.008
#> Version: robust (auto: the fit uses FIML (missing = "ml"))

# Rotation to a partially specified target, through efa_k(), the same
# function under a shorter name, here of the minimum residual (minres)
# solution: unweighted least squares on the correlation matrix, with
# sandwich standard errors from the raw data. Each item is targeted at
# zero on the factor it is not keyed to, and the items and the number of
# factors are read from the target.
efa_k(holzinger_swineford, rotation = "target", estimator = "ULS",
      seed = 113, target = list(spatial = items[1:3], verbal = items[4:6]))
#> Exploratory factor analysis: 2 factors, 6 items, N = 301
#> Estimator: ULS (minimum residual: unweighted least squares on the correlation matrix); missing data: listwise deletion; rotation: target (oblique), 6 of 12 loadings specified (all 0); SE: sandwich with the normal theory covariance matrix of the correlations (robust.sem.nt)
#> 
#>                        item                      f1                      f2
#>        t1_visual_perception    0.562 [0.393, 0.732]    0.185 [0.066, 0.304]
#>                    t2_cubes    0.459 [0.306, 0.613]   0.014 [-0.118, 0.145]
#>                 t4_lozenges    0.783 [0.624, 0.942] -0.132 [-0.206, -0.059]
#>  t6_paragraph_comprehension   0.038 [-0.036, 0.112]    0.834 [0.774, 0.894]
#>                 t7_sentence -0.089 [-0.153, -0.025]    0.905 [0.853, 0.957]
#>             t9_word_meaning    0.086 [0.012, 0.160]    0.796 [0.739, 0.854]
#>           communality complexity
#>  0.428 [0.260, 0.596]      1.213
#>  0.216 [0.100, 0.332]      1.002
#>  0.554 [0.325, 0.782]      1.057
#>  0.721 [0.637, 0.805]      1.004
#>  0.766 [0.691, 0.842]      1.019
#>  0.693 [0.617, 0.769]      1.023
#> (standardized pattern loadings and communalities with 95% intervals, and Hofmann's complexity; tidy(x) has every parameter in both metrics)
#> 
#> Target (the value where a loading is specified, ? where it is not):
#>                            f1 f2
#> t1_visual_perception        ?  0
#> t2_cubes                    ?  0
#> t4_lozenges                 ?  0
#> t6_paragraph_comprehension  0  ?
#> t7_sentence                 0  ?
#> t9_word_meaning             0  ?
#> Factors: f1 = spatial, f2 = verbal (the table keeps lavaan's names).
#> 
#> Variance accounted for (sums of squared standardized loadings, the diagonal of Phi Lambda' Lambda):
#>  factor sum_sq_loadings proportion_variance proportion_common
#>      f1           1.167               0.195             0.346
#>      f2           2.210               0.368             0.654
#>   total           3.378               0.563             1.000
#> 
#> Factor correlations with 95% intervals:
#>                      f1                   f2
#> f1                    1 0.374 [0.239, 0.509]
#> f2 0.374 [0.239, 0.509]                    1
#> 
#> Factor determinacy and coefficient H with 95% intervals:
#>  factor          determinacy                min_r                    H
#>      f1 0.840 [0.786, 0.883] 0.411 [0.234, 0.558] 0.700 [0.567, 0.806]
#>      f2 0.944 [0.933, 0.954] 0.784 [0.740, 0.821] 0.896 [0.865, 0.920]
#> (determinacy: the correlation of the regression factor score with its factor, whose square is the factor's maximal reliability; min_r: the lowest correlation two sets of scores equally consistent with the model can have, 2 x determinacy^2 - 1 (Guttman, 1955); H: Hancock and Mueller's reliability of the optimally weighted composite from the factor's loadings alone; limits from the logit scale)
#> 
#> Fit: ULS discrepancy statistic 0.373 on 4 df (no reference distribution, so no p-value, RMSEA, CFI, or TLI); NFI 0.999; SRMR 0.008
#> Version: standard (auto: a ULS fit of complete data with the standard test alone, whose statistic lavaan gives no reference distribution and which is the ULS discrepancy of a correlation structure)
#> Chi square: standard
#> The fit_measures attribute holds every measure with its version lines.
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> The minimum residual solution is unweighted least squares fitted to the correlation matrix. The ULS statistic has no chi square reference distribution: in the fit_measures attribute the chi_square row is N - 1 times the ULS discrepancy without a p-value, the RMSEA, CFI, TLI, RNI, and IFI are NA, and the NFI and SRMR are reported. Intervals condition on the selected factor count and on a target fixed before the data were seen; a target revised after seeing a rotation makes the analysis exploratory.
